name: Arabic
facts: Official or national language in over 20 countries across North Africa and the Middle East, the Arab world.
Modern Standard Arabic, used in writing and formal speech, differs widely from everyday spoken dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf and Maghrebi Arabic.
Written right-to-left in the Arabic script; it is the liturgical language of Islam and the language of the Quran.
Has given many loanwords to other languages, including Spanish, Swahili and Persian.

name: Berber
facts: Covers a family of closely related varieties spoken across North Africa and the Sahara, including Kabyle (Algeria), Tashelhit and Tarifit (Morocco), and Tuareg (Sahel).
Co-official with Arabic in Morocco and Algeria since constitutional reforms in the 2000s–2010s.
Has its own ancient alphabet, Tifinagh, though Latin and Arabic scripts are also widely used today.
Spoken by indigenous Amazigh (Berber) peoples who predate the Arab conquest of North Africa.

name: Amharic
facts: The working/federal language of Ethiopia and native tongue of the Amhara people, centred on the Amhara region and Addis Ababa.
Written in the Ge'ez script, a unique syllabary also used for Tigrinya; it reads left to right.
A Semitic language despite being spoken deep in East Africa, related to Hebrew and Arabic.
Second most spoken Semitic language in the world after Arabic.

name: Oromo
facts: Most widely spoken native language in Ethiopia, the language of the Oromo people in the Oromia region surrounding Addis Ababa.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin-based Qubee alphabet since 1991.
Also spoken by Oromo communities in northern Kenya.
One of Ethiopia's federally recognised working languages alongside Amharic.

name: Tigrinya
facts: Main language of Eritrea, the country's largest working language, and of Ethiopia's Tigray region.
Written in the Ge'ez script, shared with Amharic and Tigre.
Closely related to Tigre and more distantly to Amharic; it descends from the ancient Semitic language Ge'ez.
The 1998–2000 and 2020–2022 Ethiopia–Eritrea/Tigray conflicts were fought largely in Tigrinya-speaking areas.

name: Somali
facts: National language of Somalia and Somaliland, also spoken across the Somali-inhabited Horn of Africa in Ethiopia, Kenya and Djibouti.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin alphabet (Somali script) adopted officially in 1972.
Has an unusually rich oral poetry tradition, sometimes called a 'nation of poets'.
One of the few African languages spoken natively by a single ethnic group across several modern state borders.

name: Afar
facts: Spoken by the Afar people across the arid Afar Triangle: the Afar Region of Ethiopia, Djibouti, and coastal Eritrea.
A Cushitic language, written in the Latin alphabet; traditionally has no single standardized orthography across all regions.
The Afar Region of Ethiopia includes the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest and lowest places on Earth.
Co-official regional language alongside French and Arabic in Djibouti's administration.

name: Tigre
facts: Spoken by the Tigre people mainly in the Gash-Barka and northern lowland regions of Eritrea.
A Semitic language closer to the ancient Ge'ez than Tigrinya or Amharic are, but not mutually intelligible with Tigrinya despite the similar name.
Traditionally written in the Ge'ez script; some communities also use Arabic script.
Most speakers are Muslim, unlike the mostly Christian Tigrinya speakers to the south.

name: Swahili
facts: A Bantu language with heavy Arabic influence, native to the Swahili coast of Tanzania and Kenya, and a lingua franca across East Africa.
Official language of Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, and the African Union; co-official in the DR Congo and Rwanda.
Developed as a trade language along the Indian Ocean coast through centuries of contact between Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab traders.
Written in the Latin alphabet today, though historically also in Arabic script (Kiswahili cha Kiarabu).

name: Hausa
facts: Most widely spoken language of the Sahel, concentrated in northern Nigeria and southern Niger.
A Chadic branch of the Afroasiatic family; traditionally written in Ajami (Arabic script) as well as the Latin-based Boko alphabet.
Major lingua franca of West African trade, spoken as a second language far beyond its core states.
Kano, Nigeria's second-largest city, is the historic heart of Hausa culture and commerce.

name: Yoruba
facts: Spoken by the Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria, centred on Lagos, Ibadan and Oyo, with communities in Benin and Togo.
A tonal language with three pitch tones; small diacritic marks show the tones in writing.
Carried to the Americas by the slave trade, it shaped Afro-Caribbean religions such as Santería and Candomblé.
Has a rich tradition of oral praise poetry (oriki) and drum-based talking communication.

name: Igbo
facts: Spoken by the Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria, centred on Anambra, Imo, Abia, Enugu and Ebonyi states.
A tonal language with numerous dialects; a standard literary form was developed in the 20th century.
The former short-lived state of Biafra (1967–1970) was based in Igbo-speaking territory.
Chinua Achebe, author of Things Fall Apart, was a native Igbo speaker and drew heavily on Igbo culture.

name: Fula
facts: Spoken by the Fula (Fulani) people, traditionally cattle-herding, scattered in communities across the Sahel from Senegal to Sudan — one of the widest ranges of any African language.
Largest single ethnic group in Guinea, centred on the Fouta Djallon highlands; also a large minority in Senegal, Mali, Nigeria and Cameroon.
Belongs to the Senegambian branch of Niger–Congo, related to Wolof and Serer, and has grammatical noun classes marked by consonant changes.
Historically written in Arabic-based Ajami script before the modern Latin alphabet.

name: Wolof
facts: Native language of the Wolof people and the de facto lingua franca of Senegal, understood by around 90% of the population.
Also spoken in the Gambia and southern Mauritania.
Not Senegal's official language (that is French), but its most widely spoken, including in Dakar's street culture and music (mbalax).
Belongs to the Senegambian branch of Niger–Congo, related to Fula and Serer.

name: Bambara
facts: National lingua franca of Mali, understood by most of the population even where it is not the first language.
Part of the Manding group of Mande languages, mutually intelligible with Dioula/Malinke across Mali, Guinea and Ivory Coast.
Traditionally also written in the N'Ko alphabet, invented in 1949 specifically for Manding languages.
Centred on Bamako and the Niger River heartland of southern Mali.

name: Akan
facts: Most widely spoken indigenous language of Ghana; Twi and Fante are its two main varieties.
Akwaaba, the Twi word for 'welcome', is widely recognised across Ghana.
A Kwa branch Niger–Congo language, tonal, written in a Latin-based alphabet since the 19th century.
The historic Ashanti Empire, centred on Kumasi, was an Akan-speaking kingdom.

name: Ewe
facts: Spoken by the Ewe people across the Volta Region of Ghana, Togo, and southwestern Benin.
A tonal Kwa language with a tradition of drum-based talking and praise poetry similar to neighbouring Akan.
Shares part of its homeland with and is closely related to Fon, spoken mainly in Benin.
Written in a Latin-based alphabet standardized in the colonial period.

name: Mooré
facts: Native language of the Mossi people, the largest ethnic group in Burkina Faso, and the country's most widely spoken language.
Centred on the old Mossi kingdoms and the capital Ouagadougou.
A Gur (Voltaic) branch Niger–Congo language, tonal, written in the Latin alphabet.
French remains Burkina Faso's official language, but Mooré is the common everyday lingua franca.

name: Kanuri
facts: Spoken around Lake Chad by the Kanuri people, centred on Borno State in northeastern Nigeria, the historic Kanem-Bornu Empire.
A Saharan branch Nilo-Saharan language, unrelated to its neighbouring Niger–Congo and Chadic languages.
Written both in a Latin-based orthography and in Arabic-derived Ajami script.
Kanem-Bornu was one of the oldest and longest-lived states in African history, lasting from roughly the 9th to the 19th century.

name: Lingala
facts: A Bantu lingua franca of the Congo River basin, widely used in Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo's army, and popular Congolese music (soukous).
Also one of the national languages of the Republic of the Congo, across the river from Kinshasa.
Developed in the 19th century from a riverine trade language as colonial and missionary activity spread it widely.
One of four national languages of the DR Congo alongside Kikongo, Tshiluba and Swahili, French being the official language.

name: Kongo
facts: Language of the historic Kingdom of Kongo, spoken around the Congo River mouth in western DR Congo, Angola's Cabinda/Zaire provinces, and the Republic of the Congo.
A Bantu language; its speakers' descendants, taken in the slave trade, carried Kikongo-derived words and traditions to the Americas (e.g. into Haitian Creole and Kumina in Jamaica).
One of the DR Congo's four recognised national languages.
Closely related to, but distinct from, Lingala, the other major lingua franca of the lower Congo River region.

name: Luba-Kasai
facts: Also called Tshiluba, spoken by the Luba people of the Kasai region in south-central DR Congo.
One of the DR Congo's four national languages alongside Lingala, Kikongo and Swahili.
A Bantu language, tonal, used widely in Kananga and Mbuji-Mayi, major cities of the Kasai provinces.
The diamond-mining region of Kasai gives Tshiluba speakers an outsized role in the Congolese economy.

name: Kinyarwanda
facts: National and official language of Rwanda, spoken by virtually the entire population regardless of ethnicity.
A Bantu language, nearly mutually intelligible with Kirundi, spoken just across the border in Burundi.
Also spoken by Rwandan communities in eastern DR Congo (North Kivu).
One of the few African languages with near-universal national monolingual coverage within its country.

name: Kirundi
facts: National and official language of Burundi, spoken by nearly the entire population.
A Bantu language, closely related to and largely mutually intelligible with Kinyarwanda across the border in Rwanda.
Tonal, with a complex noun-class system typical of Bantu languages.
Amahoro, meaning 'peace', is a common greeting and a frequent theme in post-conflict Burundian public life.

name: Luganda
facts: Language of the Buganda kingdom, centred on the capital Kampala, and the most widely spoken local language in Uganda.
A Bantu language serving as an everyday lingua franca across much of southern and central Uganda, alongside the official English.
Buganda is Uganda's largest traditional kingdom, with its own king (Kabaka) still recognised as a cultural institution.
Noun classes and extensive vowel-length distinctions are characteristic features of its grammar.

name: Kikuyu
facts: Largest single ethnic language of Kenya, spoken by the Kikuyu people of the Central region around Mount Kenya.
A Bantu language, closely related to Embu and Meru, the neighbouring peoples of the same highland area.
The Mau Mau uprising against British colonial rule in the 1950s was centred in Kikuyu-speaking areas.
Many of Kenya's post-independence political and business elite have come from the Kikuyu community.

name: Luo
facts: Spoken by the Luo people around Lake Victoria in western Kenya's Nyanza region, and across the lake in northern Tanzania.
A Nilotic language, unlike most of its Bantu-speaking Kenyan neighbours, reflecting Luo migration south from South Sudan centuries ago.
Has no grammatical tones for lexical meaning but uses them for grammar, unlike many Niger–Congo languages.
Barack Obama's father was a Luo speaker from western Kenya.

name: Zulu
facts: Most widely spoken home language in South Africa, native to KwaZulu-Natal and the Zulu kingdom founded by Shaka in the early 19th century.
A Bantu language famous for its click consonants, borrowed from neighbouring Khoisan languages.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages, and widely understood as a second language across the country.
Sawubona, literally 'we see you', is a well-known Zulu greeting.

name: Xhosa
facts: Native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa; like Zulu, it borrows distinctive click consonants from Khoisan languages.
Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki were both native Xhosa speakers.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages, widely spoken in Cape Town and the Western Cape as well as the Eastern Cape.
Closely related to Zulu; the two are partly mutually intelligible.

name: Afrikaans
facts: Descended from 17th-century Dutch brought by settlers to the Cape, with influences from Khoisan, Malay, Portuguese and African languages.
Mutually intelligible to a large extent with Dutch, though with simplified grammar.
Widely spoken as a first language among both white Afrikaner and Cape Coloured communities, especially in the Western and Northern Cape.
Also an official and widely spoken language in neighbouring Namibia, a former South African territory.

name: Sotho
facts: National language of Lesotho, a kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa, and also one of South Africa's 12 official languages.
Centred on South Africa's Free State province and the whole of Lesotho.
A Bantu language closely related to Tswana and Northern Sotho, with mutual intelligibility between them.
Lesotho's near-total ethnic homogeneity makes Sesotho one of Africa's most universally spoken national languages.

name: Tswana
facts: National and majority language of Botswana, where almost all citizens speak it either as a first or second language.
Also official and spoken in South Africa's North West province, bordering Botswana.
A Bantu language closely related to Sotho and Northern Sotho (the Sotho-Tswana group).
English remains Botswana's official language of government, but Setswana dominates daily and cultural life.

name: Northern Sotho
facts: Also known as Sepedi, centred on South Africa's Limpopo province.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages and among the five most widely spoken.
A Bantu language of the Sotho-Tswana group, closely related to Southern Sotho and Tswana.
Named Sepedi after the historic Pedi kingdom, though the language covers several related Northern Sotho dialects.

name: Tsonga
facts: Spoken by the Tsonga people across South Africa's Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces and southern Mozambique.
One of South Africa's 12 official languages.
A Bantu language; called Changana in Mozambique, where it is a widely spoken trade language in the south.
Closely related to, but distinct from, the Shona languages spoken further north.

name: Swati
facts: National language of Eswatini (formerly Swaziland), one of Africa's last remaining monarchies.
Also one of South Africa's 12 official languages, spoken in Mpumalanga near the Eswatini border.
A Bantu language closely related to Zulu, with similar click consonants and grammar.
Nearly the entire population of Eswatini speaks siSwati as a first language.

name: Shona
facts: Most widely spoken home language of Zimbabwe, used across most of the country except the southwest.
A Bantu language, named after the Shona people; the medieval stone city of Great Zimbabwe was built by Shona-speaking ancestors.
Written in a Latin-based orthography standardized in the 20th century from several related dialects.
Also spoken by communities in Mozambique's Manica province, bordering Zimbabwe.

name: Northern Ndebele
facts: Spoken in Matabeleland in southwestern Zimbabwe, centred on the city of Bulawayo.
A Bantu language closely related to Zulu; Ndebele groups migrated north from Zululand in the 19th century under Mzilikazi.
Distinct from the Southern Ndebele language spoken in South Africa's Mpumalanga province, though related.
One of Zimbabwe's 16 officially recognised languages, second in speakers only to Shona.

name: Chichewa
facts: National language of Malawi, spoken by the large majority of the population as mother tongue or lingua franca.
Known as Nyanja in Zambia and Mozambique, where it is also an important lingua franca.
A Bantu language with a well-developed literary tradition and its own radio broadcasting history dating to colonial times.
Named after the Chewa people, historically linked to the Maravi Empire around Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa).

name: Bemba
facts: Most widely spoken Zambian language, centred on the Copperbelt and Northern provinces.
A Bantu language used widely as a lingua franca across Zambia's mining towns, beyond its home region.
English is Zambia's official language, but Bemba is one of several recognised regional languages used in media and schools.
Closely related to other Bantu languages of the wider Luba-Bemba cultural cluster spanning Zambia and southern DR Congo.

name: Umbundu
facts: Spoken by the Ovimbundu, Angola's largest ethnic group, centred on the central highlands around Huambo and Benguela.
A Bantu language; most speakers are also fluent in Portuguese, Angola's official language.
Historically tied to the Benguela highland kingdoms and 19th-century caravan trade routes to the coast.
Despite being the largest Angolan ethnic language by speaker numbers, it has no official status nationally.

name: Malagasy
facts: National language of Madagascar, remarkably an Austronesian language, not an African one, brought by seafarers from Borneo roughly 1,500–2,000 years ago.
Closely related to Ma'anyan, a language of southern Borneo, far across the Indian Ocean.
Written in the Latin alphabet since the 19th century, replacing an earlier Arabic-derived Sorabe script used on the island.
Shows later layers of Bantu, Arabic and French loanwords from later waves of contact.

name: Sango
facts: National language and lingua franca of the Central African Republic, spoken as a first or second language by nearly everyone.
A creole that developed from Ngbandi, a local Niger–Congo language, mixed through river trade along the Ubangi.
French remains the official language of government and higher education, but Sango dominates daily communication.
Despite being spoken natively by relatively few, it functions as a true national lingua franca across dozens of local ethnic languages.

name: Krio
facts: English-based creole that is the lingua franca of Sierra Leone, spoken as a first language mainly in and around Freetown.
Originated among freed and resettled slaves brought to Freetown from Britain, Nova Scotia and the Caribbean from 1787 onward.
Although spoken natively by a minority, it is understood by almost all Sierra Leoneans as a second language.
English remains the official language, but Krio is the dominant everyday spoken language across the country.
